Eli Lilly grew revenue 48% last quarter, showing longevity science delivers real returns today while nuclear energy plays won't produce meaningful revenue until 2029.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.13% on October 21. That is already above the ceiling Alan Rechtschaffen expects for long-term rates. On the same day, UBS weighed in. UBS's senior portfolio manager laid out a case for the S&P 500 to reach 9,500 by June 2027.

Shutterstock

His target sits well above the UBS base case of 8,400 and above his own call for 8,100 by the end of 2026. He ties it to three long-running technology waves: superintelligence, longevity and disease cures, and energy.

Profits are his strongest evidence. He cited 25% year-over-year earnings growth. He expects double-digit gains next year, so the rally rests on what companies actually earn.

His rate path complicates the outlook. He expects the Fed to pause in October, probably raise rates in December and again in March, and only then consider cuts. A bull case that runs through two more hikes requires you to trust that productivity gains will outrun tighter money.

Profits Are Carrying This Rally

Earnings-driven gains hold up better than price-to-earnings expansion, because multiples can shrink quickly when rates move. For NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), fiscal second-quarter revenue grew 105.8% to $96.22 billion, with Data Center sales of $89.02 billion.

At Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Azure grew 43% and passed $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time. Google Cloud revenue at Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL) jumped 82%.

Double-digit growth next year depends on that spending continuing to turn into revenue. NVIDIA expects supply to remain a bottleneck at least through the end of fiscal year '28. That points to strong demand, but it also caps how fast the company can ship.

title: How much MSFT stock does Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella actually own?
detail:
How much MSFT stock does Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella actually own?
Laura Rodini, Jeremy Salvucci
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 10:07 AM MST 4 min read
MSFT
NOK
OPAI.PVT
AAPL
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Not many people remember this, but when Satya Nadella took the reins as CEO of Microsoft in February 2014, the company was struggling to find its place amidst a tech landscape dominated by Apple's smartphones, Google's Android operating system, and Amazon's cloud computing services.

Under the leadership of Steve Ballmer, Microsoft had undertaken a contentious $7.2 billion acquisition of Nokia's mobile phone business in 2013. That deal ultimately failed, resulting in billions in write-downs and thousands of layoffs.

But Nadella did not turn the company around overnight. Over the next few years, he shifted Microsoft's business model even further into cloud computing by expanding Azure and its subscription-based services. He also made strategic acquisitions, including LinkedIn, GitHub, and Minecraft, while investing billions into artificial intelligence before it became a household name.

In fact, you could say that Nadella was instrumental in Microsoft's partnership with OpenAI, as he even personally stepped in to serve as mediator when OpenAI's board briefly fired its CEO and co-founder, Sam Altman, in the fall of 2023.

Although Microsoft and OpenAI renegotiated their once-exclusive partnership, Microsoft hasn't lost momentum. Their newest agreement, announced in April 2026, gave each greater independence and allowed Microsoft to continue to expand its own AI capabilities through Azure's cloud services.

MSFT crossed the trillion-dollar valuation threshold on April 25, 2019, and it hasn't looked back since. In its most recent earnings, the company reported that Azure revenue grew by 43% year-over-year. These results show that Microsoft isn't just one of the founders of the digital era — it's very much a power player, and as the driver behind its innovation, Nadella himself has been rewarded handsomely through salary increases, bonuses, and enormous stock awards.

How much of MSFT does Satya Nadella own? Is he the biggest inividual shareholder?

As of Microsoft's latest Proxy statement for fiscal 2025, filed in September 2025, Satya Nadella owned 900,572 shares of Microsoft, equating to about 0.01% of the company's total outstanding shares.

Given MSFT's October 19 closing share price of $533.52, those shares would be worth a whopping $480.4 million.

But Nadella isn't Microsoft's biggest individual shareholder — not by a long shot.

That distinction actually belongs to Steve Ballmer, who is estimated to still own approximately 319 million shares, or roughly 4% of Microsoft. Despite Ballmer stepping down amid Microsoft's struggles, he still owns more than 350 times as much as Nadella's stake.

Microsoft, Google parent and McDonald’s protest new trading plan
Anand Sinha

Top publicly listed companies such as Microsoft (Nasdaq: MSFT), Google parent Alphabet (Nasdaq: GOOGL), Coreweave (Nasdaq: CRWV), Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS), and McDonald's (NYSE: MCD) have joined hands to protest the inclusion of the tokenized version of their stocks on the OKXICE TSV.

As per the public notice issued Oct. 19, the number of companies objecting to the plan is 16, demonstrating growing opposition to the tokenization trend.

What Microsoft, Alphabet, and McDonald's are opposing

The companies' protest centres on OKXICE issuing the tokenized version of their stocks.

In simple words, tokenization is the process of using blockchain technology to turn real‑world assets like stocks, real estate, U.S. Treasury bills, etc. into digital tokens which can be traded fractionally, 24/7.

Crypto companies such as Coinbase Global (Nasdaq: COIN), Robinhood Markets (Nasdaq: HOOD), and OKXICE are at the forefront of the tokenization trend.

The tokenized stocks are advantageous to traders who want to buy and sell shares 24/7. They also offer exposure to those from outside the U.S. who don't have access to avenues like the Nasdaq and the NYSE.

But they don't offer shareholder rights such as ownership and voting like original stocks do.

OKXICE TSV is a proposed tokenized stock trading platform created by OKXICE, a 50-50 joint venture between the NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange and crypto exchange OKX.

The avenue will operate under the innovation exemption published last month by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The exemption lets such platforms offer tokenized versions of the U.S. stocks without registering as exchanges.

The latest notice doesn't explain the companies' reasons or if their objection stops TSV from issuing the tokens. However, it says these tokens could be issued by an outside party or the issuer itself, which could give companies a more direct role in the process.

title: How Unusual Is Box's Latest Profit Margin?

Box, Inc. (BOX) now keeps 9.4 cents of every dollar of sales after the costs of running its business. The company sells what it calls an intelligent content management platform to businesses, and its operating margin over the twelve months to July 2026 is the highest it has been in ten years. A record sounds impressive, but it means little until you know where Box usually sits. So what would you guess Box's margin usually is?

How Unusual Is This For Box?

The current figure is very unusual, because Box ran at a loss for much of the past ten years. It has made an operating profit in every twelve-month period since the one to October 2022. Measured at all 40 quarter-ends over the past ten years, not just the ten shown below, its median twelve-month operating margin was a loss of 3.1%, against a profit of 9.4% now.

Box passed its previous record of 8.6%, set in the twelve months to April 2026. This marks the second quarter-end in a row at a new high.

What Is Behind Box's Record Profit Margin?

Box has been selling more at higher prices to its existing customers, while its costs have grown more slowly than its sales. Management credited the latest quarter to rapid customer adoption of Enterprise Advanced, and named a major federal agency among the customers that upgraded to it from Enterprise Plus. Box's net retention rate improved to 106% from 103% a year earlier, driven by both price per seat increases and seat expansion.

Suites customers now account for 69% of revenue, up from 63% a year ago, management said on the August 25, 2026 call. Sales have also grown from a year earlier in each of the last 40 quarters.

Is The Latest Quarter Still Improving?

Yes, by 1.2 percentage points. In fiscal Q2 2027, the quarter to July 2026, Box's operating margin was 10.2%, up from 9.0% in the quarter before and 7.0% in the same quarter a year earlier.

You can ask whether that is a good margin, but the better question is which way Box is moving. A twelve-month figure moves slowly and can keep rising after the quarters inside it start to slip. Box's latest quarter has not slipped. It beat the previous quarter and sits above the twelve-month figure, so the newest quarter is still pushing the record up.

Dividend investing will never go out of style, and for good reason. Buying shares of companies that pay and consistently raise their dividends is a great way to earn long-term returns, as it allows investors to put the magic of compounding to work through dividend reinvestment. Of course, dividend stocks come in all shapes and sizes, and some of them aren't worth the trouble for long-term investors. Let's consider three that are worth investing in: Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), and Visa (NYSE:V).

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

1. Coca-Cola

Coca-Cola boasts one of the most popular brands in the world. The company has a large beverage portfolio across multiple categories and generates consistent revenue and earnings. Coca-Cola has been doing it for a while, and over the long run, it has avoided becoming an irrelevant company by keeping up with changing consumer tastes and preferences.

Coca-Cola has introduced new products, innovative twists on old products, and acquired new brands. These efforts have allowed it to remain one of the top players in its industry, and there is more to come. Coca-Cola estimates that it accounts for 2.2 billion of the 65 billion daily beverage servings worldwide.

Increased sales volume and market share gains could help the company grow its revenue and earnings, and we have seen the consumer staples giant pull that off this year. In the second quarter, the company grew its share of the non-alcoholic ready-to-drink beverage market. That's just one quarter, but Coca-Cola appears well-positioned to maintain consistent revenue and earnings growth over the long run. Finally, the company has a fantastic dividend track record.

Coca-Cola is a Dividend King. These are companies with 50 or more consecutive annual dividend increases. Coca-Cola's streak is at 64, and it seems unlikely to end soon, making the stock a great pick for long-term income seekers.

2. Microsoft

Microsoft has rebounded over the past few months, after hitting a brand new 52-week low in June. Some investors worry that artificial intelligence (AI) will replace the company's services, even as it spends fortunes on the technology. But Microsoft's latest quarterly update showed signs that the company is adapting to the new AI world order.

Vanguard just updated its key holdings across major exchange-traded funds (ETFs) like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO) and Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF (NYSEMKT: VUG).

As of Sept. 30, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF had a staggering 30.8% weighting in just five stocks -- Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), and Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN). Those same five companies make up a mind-numbing 49.2% of the Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Concentration in just a handful of companies may be unappealing for investors who already own mega-cap growth stocks as individual stock holdings or through ETFs and index funds.

Here's why the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (NYSEMKT: VTI) offers a superior alternative to the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF and Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF for investors who still want low-cost exposure to a basket of stocks but with less concentration in a handful of names.

Image source: Getty Images.
The Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF holds 3,519 stocks

The Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF is benchmarked to the Morningstar U.S. Total Market Index. The index holds 100% of investable U.S. equities -- from mega caps like Nvidia and Apple all the way down to small-cap and micro-caps you've probably never heard of.

Despite holding roughly seven times as many stocks as the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF is still heavily concentrated in a handful of names. For example, it has a 27.2% combined weighting in Nvidia, Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon, and a 36% combined weighting in just ten stocks. The largest U.S. companies have contributed outsized gains in recent years. The S&P 500 now makes up roughly 80% of the total U.S. stock market. So while the Total Stock Market ETF is more diverse than the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, it still has roughly 80% of its weightings in the S&P 500. Meaning that its performance will vary only slightly from the index.

You can see this pattern play out over the long-term returns. The S&P 500 ETF has a 12.9% year-to-date (YTD) return, only slightly outpacing the Total Stock Market ETF's 12.5% YTD return. Over the last five years, the S&P 500 ETF has produced an 83% total return compared to a 73.2% total return for the Total Stock Market ETF because the S&P 500 significantly outperformed the other 20% of the U.S. stock market over that period.
